newsitem.title: IRAN: Rafsanjani tells Iranians it's duty to vote.
newsitem.headline: Rafsanjani tells Iranians it's duty to vote.

text.p: President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani told Iranians on Friday it was their duty to vote in next week's election to replace him -- even those who do not support the Islamic government.
But he refrained from endorsing any of the four men vying for his job in next Friday's polls and told government officials they should not publicly back anyone either.
"I do not even tell my children who I am going to vote for," the 62-year-old Shi'ite Moslem clergyman said.

The crowd of thousands of mostly men in black shirts assembled at Tehran university for the climax of the Shi'ite mourning month of Muharram included some of Rafsanjani's cabinet ministers and two of the four candidates seeking election.
Rafsanjani, who must step down in August after eight years in office, asked the candidates to observe the law and not denigrate their rivals.

"Even those who do not support us should know that a high number of votes is to the benefit of the country and the disappointment of our enemies," he said in a 50-minute sermon at the weekly prayer session on the university campus.
He said there was no justification before God for presenting a bad image of any the four candidates, who were approved by a powerful body of clerics and lawyers out of 238 contenders.

He cautioned officials against abusing their position to influence the votes and said: "Maybe some officials think that it is better for the country to have a president who they deem deserving but such an act is the biggest crime.
"We have always won our battles with the people's trust. Why should we plant doubt into the hearts of people so they will wonder whether the elections are truly free or not?
"Changing people's votes or deflecting the healthy trend of the elections is an unforgiveable treason."

The remarks came as Rafsanjani's centrist backers have accused state radio and television of giving free publicity to parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri and ignoring the candidate backed by them -- former culture and Islamic guidance minister Mohammad Khatami.
The sermon coincided with the eve of Ashoura when Shi'ite Moslems grieve over the death in battle 13 centuries ago of Prophet Mohammad's grandson Hussein.

In black clerical robes and white turban, Rafsanjani's voice trembled with emotion as he recounted the killing of Hussein at Karbala, in modern-day Iraq, in 680. With one hand on the barrel of a rifle, he dabbed tears with the other.
Rafsanjani said Iran had proved it could stand on its own feet and did not need to rely on the United States and was a role model for all Moslem countries.
He referred to a agreement signed this week by Iran, Turkey and Turkmenistan on a 1,420 km (888 mile) natural gas pipeline which is part of a $23 billion accord between Tehran and Ankara.
"This was what the Americans have been opposing for the past five years and using threats and pressure to stops it.
"When in that meeting before dozens of journalists three presidents officially signed such an important agreement it proved that America had missed its target," he said.
The crowd broke into repeated chants of "Death to America", denouncing the Islamic republic's arch-foe.
Minutes earlier, a renowned reciter of devotional verse had brought the crowd to a peak of emotion as he delivered an epic poem about the martyrdom of Hussein, the third Shi'ite Imam.
Men sobbed, shook and held their heads in their hands, then stood and rhythmically beat their chests.

The two candidates present at the prayers were Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri and Reza Zavarei, who are considered to be lagging behind Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri and former culture minister Mohammad Khatami in the race.
